# Education in Australia
Education in Australia is regulated primarily by state and territory governments, with federal involvement mainly in funding and tertiary education oversight. The Australian Qualifications Framework (established in 1995) unifies qualifications across school, vocational, and higher education sectors. The national Australian Curriculum has been progressively implemented since 2010 for primary and secondary schools. Compulsory schooling ages vary across states but typically begin between ages five and six and continue until around 15 to 17 years.
Preschool education, focusing on early childhood learning, is widely attended but not mandatory, generally serving children aged three to five. Primary education covers from pre-Year 1 to Year 6, focusing on foundational literacy and numeracy, while secondary education (Year 7 to Year 12) progressively specializes subjects and offers various pathways, including vocational and academic streams. In 2023, government schools educated 64% of students, with Catholic and independent schools educating most of the remainder.
Australia features diverse school types including comprehensive government schools, selective schools that admit students based on academic criteria, specialist schools focusing on arts or sports, special schools serving students with disabilities, and international schools offering foreign curricula. Both single-sex and co-educational schools are common, with most private schools charging tuition fees that can vary widely.
Tertiary education comprises 42 universities (mostly public) and numerous vocational and training providers. Australia has a significant international student population, with international education a major export sector. Universities are globally competitive with many ranked highly in world rankings. The government subsidizes tertiary education through a loan system (HECS) repayable once incomes reach a threshold.
National assessments such as NAPLAN test students in literacy and numeracy at key stages, while international assessments like PISA gauge Australia's global education standing. Australia has experienced a decline in some educational performance measures but maintains a high Education Index rating globally. Challenges include funding adequacy, educational disparities particularly for Indigenous students, bilingual education maintenance in Indigenous communities, and school violence. Recent reforms include agreements to improve equitable school funding and ongoing efforts to enhance Indigenous educational outcomes.
